slides.heading: Truth Tables in Code
slides.body: Truth Tables in Code is part of Boolean Logic and Comparisons. This short lesson gives you a practical Python idea you can understand, try, and reuse in simple programs.

slides.heading: Core Idea: Truth Tables in Code
slides.body: A truth table shows how boolean operators behave for different True and False combinations. It helps you predict logic before coding.

slides.heading: Real-World Analogy
slides.body: A truth table is like a checklist grid showing what happens for every possible pair of answers.

slides.heading: Example: Truth Tables in Code
slides.code:
a = True
b = False
print(a or b)

slides.heading: Key Rule
slides.body: Boolean expressions must produce True or False. Use comparisons and logical operators carefully.

slides.heading: Try It Yourself!
slides.prompt: Print the result of True and False.

quiz.prompt_text: What is the result of True and False in Python?
quiz.explanation: Well done! True and False evaluates to False because the and operator requires both values to be True. If either is False, the result is False.

quiz.prompt_text: Arrange the following lines to set two boolean variables and evaluate them with or.
quiz.explanation: a is assigned first, then b is assigned False, and finally or checks whether at least one is True. Since a is True, the result is True.

quiz.prompt_text: Print the result of the expression True and False to verify what the and operator returns.
quiz.correct_answer: Any valid Python code that satisfies the prompt.
quiz.explanation: print(True and False) outputs False. The and operator needs both values to be True. This matches the truth table entry: T AND F = F.
